# Steam bulk carrying dominant

Liverpool University Press eBooks. Published: 2023-05-12. Book chapter. 0 citations.

## Abstract

This chapter examines the developments from 1890 to 1950 during saw the steam tramp grew in size, efficiency and sophistication, and came to dominate the carriage of dry bulk cargoes and eliminate sail from long-distance trades. For the largest builder and operator, Great Britain, total tonnage of steam vessels surpassed that for sail in the 1880s. Decennial surveys reveal a growth in tonnage over this period of 140 per cent, a 380 per cent increase in ballast capacity, and a doubling of power output. Although the fundamental features of the tramp were well established by 1890, competition amongst shipbuilders resulted in considerable variations in hull structure, claimed to reduce first cost and fuel consumption, improve seaworthiness and ease trimming of cargoes. The most significant was the Doxford ‘Turret’ design, and its imitations. Although these designs were not adopted long term, the increased longitudinal strength which the ‘Turret’ hull gave was recognised as important, especially as hulls got lengthier, and this led to the adoption of the Isherwood system of longitudinal framing. The period ended with British builders and operators of steam tramps being challenged by overseas competitors.
